newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian royalist PM meets Khmer Rouge leader.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian royalist PM meets Khmer Rouge leader.

text.p: Cambodian First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh met dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary on Friday in the highest level talks to date on merging their forces.

"I told him about the real framework of national reconciliation. Ieng Sary put forward his position and the reasons that led him to join the government," Ranariddh told journalists after visiting the rebel's northwest base of Pailin.
Ieng Sary, foreign minister under the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot, asked for more time to merge his breakaway forces with the royal coalition government.

Ieng Sary broke in August with hardline Khmer Rouge forces loyal to Pol Pot and forged a ceasefire with the government, but Friday's meeting was his first with the very top echelon of the coalition government formed after U.N.-run elections in 1993.

"They have not asked for any position...at the same time they asked for more time to change, for (government) military uniforms and to receive ranks," Ranariddh said, adding that the rebels needed time to explain the switch to their rank and file.
"They told me that they really want reconciliation and peace to end the bloodshed," he said.

Commanders loyal to Ieng Sary had demanded, in peace talks in mid-September, that they be given top police and military posts in the central commands and asked that their base, Pailin, become the centre of a province under their control.
Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen rejected those demands and said the rebels could have senior regional military posts while their territory must come under government control.

Ieng Sary stalled talks in early September by demanding an amnesty for his role as foreign minister in the deaths of more than one million people during the Khmer Rouge "killing fields" era. The royal pardon was given on September 14.
"Ieng Sary said he will not ask for any role. They said they will not step back," said Ranariddh, adding that the rebels claimed to have 20,000 dependents and fighters under arms.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the deal. They had been fighting the coalition government.
